found: The world has tried it under several names - specialised workers under a supervisor, hierarchical teams, blackboard systems, stateful agents - and converges on one split: the expert is a role and a body of written knowledge; a session is a disposable worker that takes the role up. Gas Town says it outright (an agent is a persistent identity, sessions are cattle; any session can hand off and restart from its hook). Anthropic's long-running harness found compaction alone not enough and had every fresh session get up to speed from a progress file, git and a feature list; its context-engineering guide names notes outside the window as the tool for iterative work with milestones. Claude Code itself moved this way: subagents may keep a per-role MEMORY.md, and agent teams start each teammate from project context and a spawn prompt, never the lead's history, and do not restore teammates on resume. Against expertise held in a long context: models recall worse as input grows (Chroma, context rot; Anthropic's attention budget), repeated summarising erodes detail (ACE: context collapse, brevity bias), and a session of 1000-1800 messages re-reads all of it each turn - after an idle hour without the cache, at full price - so a standing expert answering an occasional question is the costliest and not the most reliable way to answer it. Against a central router: a supervisor that relays every message plays telephone - lower scores and more tokens than agents handing off directly (LangChain); misalignment between agents (lost context, withheld information) is one of the three failure groups in 1600 traces (MAST). What works (Cognition, 2026): one writer per thing, other agents adding intelligence not actions; a consult works best given a fork of the asker's full context. Blackboard systems route by a shared record agents read, not by a relay. For us: most of the audio expertise is already rows in docs (5 research, 2 decisions, 27 backlog items name the microphone); what is not written is the tacit part - dead ends, where the experiment patches are, what hung the phone - and it now lives in hand-over notes outside any repository.

found: Agents are now near-human at reading binaries (arXiv 2610.14960; 2608.11469 SRE-Bench: best agents solve ~27-32% of realistic ones), but no paper yet covers clean-room hardware bring-up; the practice does. AI "clean rooms" (ArtCraft: a rule on inputs; chardet 7.0: disputed) cannot prove the wall by the model's mind, only by what it was shown - so use an INPUT wall: observer (traces on the stock system, GPL vendor kernel source, public specs) writes spec rows with evidence kind + hash; a separate scrubber checks them for expression; the implementer sees only accepted rows, public specs and mainline; commits cite spec ids; per-session input log and taint register. Tools: mmiotrace/ftrace/dynamic debug/regmap/QMI logs/debugfs on the running stock system (Nouveau, Asahi m1n1 tracing, freedreno), never disassembly or vendor binaries (Asahi: 'without looking at the code'). Walleye: most MSM8998 parts are upstream and need no clean room; likely only panel init, sensor hub, audio calibration/topology, camera, vendor protocols. GPL vendor kernel (android-msm-wahoo, kcxt/linux-wahoo) is read and ported with licence kept - no clean room. EFF: clean room is good practice, not a legal requirement; no court has ruled on AI clean rooms. Not legal advice. Full proposal, table of parts and record design in the material.

found: Acoustically, through the paths a person uses, with the analysis in Rust: during the call the uplink capture that the call needs anyway (1 channel on TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3, the bottom mic) is written to a file instead of thrown away. The phone plays a pattern of three short tones (e.g. 800, 1300, 1900 Hz, 200 ms each, 300 ms apart - inside the 300-3400 Hz every voice codec keeps) on the loudspeaker at the manifest's quiet level; the bottom mic hears it at once (proves the injection) and sends it up the call; the echo comes back down and plays on the earpiece, and the same mic hears it again 150-1500 ms later (the network's round trip; acoustic reflections are under 20 ms). A Goertzel envelope per frequency finds the pattern twice; the echo counts when the same order of tones recurs at one delay, 15 dB above the noise, and the delay is reported. Before the echo call, a call to the tone line (99702) proves the downlink alone, so a missing echo says uplink (or the line) rather than everything. Cost: one call of at most 25 s (dial, about 8 s to answer, 5 s of pattern, hang up; a hard timeout), at most once a day, a landline-rate number: inside a flat, or under 10 ct per day on prepaid. Skips cleanly, as unknown: no modem, no SIM, not registered, no voice interface, no call path (call-audio-path failing), the daily call already made, or the number unset in the manifest. A pass proves works for modem-calls. If q6voice exposes in-call record/playback ports (downstream's VOICE_RECORD_RX, incall music), a digital loop could replace the acoustic one later; unknown on this driver.

found: The world has tried it under several names - specialised workers under a supervisor, hierarchical teams, blackboard systems, stateful agents - and converges on one split: the expert is a role and a body of written knowledge; a session is a disposable worker that takes the role up. Gas Town says it outright (an agent is a persistent identity, sessions are cattle; any session can hand off and restart from its hook). Anthropic's long-running harness found compaction alone not enough and had every fresh session get up to speed from a progress file, git and a feature list; its context-engineering guide names notes outside the window as the tool for iterative work with milestones. Claude Code itself moved this way: subagents may keep a per-role MEMORY.md, and agent teams start each teammate from project context and a spawn prompt, never the lead's history, and do not restore teammates on resume. Against expertise held in a long context: models recall worse as input grows (Chroma, context rot; Anthropic's attention budget), repeated summarising erodes detail (ACE: context collapse, brevity bias), and a session of 1000-1800 messages re-reads all of it each turn - after an idle hour without the cache, at full price - so a standing expert answering an occasional question is the costliest and not the most reliable way to answer it. Against a central router: a supervisor that relays every message plays telephone - lower scores and more tokens than agents handing off directly (LangChain); misalignment between agents (lost context, withheld information) is one of the three failure groups in 1600 traces (MAST). What works (Cognition, 2026): one writer per thing, other agents adding intelligence not actions; a consult works best given a fork of the asker's full context. Blackboard systems route by a shared record agents read, not by a relay. For us: most of the audio expertise is already rows in docs (5 research, 2 decisions, 27 backlog items name the microphone); what is not written is the tacit part - dead ends, where the experiment patches are, what hung the phone - and it now lives in hand-over notes outside any repository.

Read from the LineageOS copy of Google's wahoo kernel (4.4, branch lineage-22.2) and kcxt/linux-wahoo wahoo/5.17; observed facts only, nothing copied; table in research/google-walleye/2026-11-17/vendor-kernel-hardware-inventory.md.
Walleye is the HTC-built half of the pair: its files are under dts/htc/ and called "muskie"; one base plus one of two overlays by board revision (xa/xb/xc or xd/xe/a; our MP1 maps to one of them - not known yet). SoC MSM8998 v2.1 with PM8998, PMI8998 and PM8005.

Touch Synaptics DSX at I2C 0x20 on the BLSP1 QUP5 bus (GPIO87/88), IRQ GPIO125, reset GPIO89. Audio: WCD934x "Tavil" codec on SLIMbus, TI TAS2557 stereo speaker amp at I2C 0x4d, no jack; NXP TFA98xx amps are in the tree but disabled. Haptics TI DRV2624 (LRA 155 Hz, I2C 0x5a, reset GPIO95). LED: TI LP5562 on early revisions, PMI8998 RGB on later. Charger: PMI8998 SMB2 with Type-C PD, TPS61099 for USB host power, NXP PTN36241G redriver. Fuel gauge: PMI8998 FG gen3 with HTC battery module, 2700 mAh, 4.4 V. NFC: NXP NQ-class at 0x28 plus PN81A secure element on SPI. Fingerprint FPC1020 family (IRQ GPIO86, reset GPIO128). Wi-Fi and Bluetooth: Qualcomm WCN3990 (Bluetooth HCI on BLSP1 UART3). Cameras: two CCI sensors, rear with autofocus, OIS, EEPROM and flash, laser ranger at I2C 0x29; the sensor chips are not named in the tree (public specs: Sony IMX362 rear, IMX179 front). Pixel Visual Core ("Easel") on PCIe 0 with a BCM15602 PMIC and SPI. Storage UFS. Sensors (IMU, magnetometer, barometer, light, Hall) are not in the application processor's tree: the SLPI sensor-hub DSP owns them, firmware proprietary.
For a phone with no display: stock describes a RAM console (ramoops) at 0xa1100000, 2 MiB, plus an alternate at 0xa3800000; the mainline port uses 0xa1810000 instead and boots with console on ttyMSM1 (BLSP2 UART1) and a USB-gadget serial ttyGS0 - which address survives a reset on this phone is not known yet.

found: They agree. (1) One small entry that is always read and routes onward, saying what each target is for: llms.txt, the root AGENTS.md (nearest wins), PhotoCraft's Read/Why orientation table, Johnny.Decimal's index, datapackage.json. (2) What is always loaded is kept small: CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, no more than ten per level, llms.txt's skippable Optional. (3) Detail in stages: Skills' name and line, then body, then linked files; Claude Code loads nested CLAUDE.md only when its subtree is touched; context engineering keeps lightweight identifiers - paths, stored queries - and loads content just in time. (4) Small units with stable addresses: evergreen notes whose titles work like APIs, numbered ADRs, Wikidata's Q and P ids. (5) Facts apart from explanation: Diátaxis' reference against explanation, Wikidata statements and infoboxes beside prose. (6) One decision per record, superseded rather than deleted (Nygard, MADR). (7) Every statement is about an item by its id and cites who says so (Wikidata). (8) Views are generated from the source data (PhotoCraft's scorecard, Mintlify's llms.txt). Tensions: hierarchy against association (fixed buckets vs dense links - a small fixed index with free links beneath answers both); one file against many (concatenation does not save context; loading on demand does). No source measured how much any of it speeds an agent - the measure here is docs' own (kb-navigation-measured).

found: Through s2idle and CPU idle, not suspend to RAM: the firmware offers no PSCI system suspend, so with userspace frozen the CPUs enter their idle states, the last one down takes the cluster power domain to its deepest state (PSCI OS-initiated mode, hierarchical CPU idle), and as the cluster powers off the application processor's RPMh sleep votes are flushed to the always-on subsystem (rpmh-rsc attached to the cluster domain). The always-on subsystem then lowers CX and DDR when no processor votes for them: CX collapse (cxsd), then AOSS sleep (aosd), the floor. The SoC counts each in its own memory (rpmh-stats, read through qcom_stats), so reaching the floor is measured, not inferred. Without OS-initiated mode the cluster domain would stay always on and the votes would never flush; surya's firmware has it.
question: How does a Qualcomm phone reach its lowest power state on mainline?

found: The modem's messages (QMI over QRTR on glink) are handled even in s2idle (IRQF_NO_SUSPEND), but userspace is frozen, so nothing rings. found:
What is: four images, one kernel/dtb/initramfs, all v0 with the dtb appended to a gzipped Image (Image.gz+dtb). a (taimen offsets, os word 0) got "Booting OKAY" then silence; b (LineageOS offsets) first left fastboot (Android came back on slot b), later Load Error; c and d (a, b plus os_version 8.1.0 / patch 2020-01) both Load Error. The only difference between a and c is that header word.

What others show (not the Pixel 2 itself - nobody reports a mainline fastboot boot there):
1. The format is the accepted one. Stock ABL on the same line (Pixel 3) takes a gzipped kernel with the dtb appended in a v0 boot image (U-Boot's board doc), and postmarketOS boots blueline with exactly base 0 / kernel 0x8000 / ramdisk 0x1000000 / tags 0x100 / page 4096 / dtb appended (pmaports deviceinfo). Two differences from our images: pmaports sets second offset 0 (we use 0xf00000; second is empty, so it should not matter) and no os_version/patch level at all. So "header v0 vs what ABL expects" and "Image.gz-dtb vs Image+dtb" are not the likely cause; the os word is, if anything, the one thing we added that pmaports does not have.
2. ABL, not the kernel, picks and patches the dtb (Inoki, MSM8998 Nokia 8): DeviceTreeAppended scans the appended blobs and DeviceTreeCompatible matches qcom,msm-id, qcom,board-id and qcom,pmic-id. Our dts carries only msm-id (0x124 0x20001, as kcxt's taimen, which boots with msm-id alone); it has no board-id or pmic-id. Whether walleye's ABL accepts that is not known; the stock walleye dtb's ids are not read yet (not in the public sources reached today).
3. The bootloader merges a dtbo overlay into the dtb before the kernel starts (AOSP DTO). kcxt found the taimen bootloader refuses a mainline kernel unless the dtbo partition holds an overlay with id 2704, and flashes a stub. Stock overlays patch downstream nodes a mainline base does not have, so a failed merge is the best-fitting reading of an immediate "Load Error" that comes from the bootloader after the transfer. Not proven for walleye: the dtbo of slot b is an older LineageOS build's, its overlay table not read.
4. "Load Error" is not proof the image is bad. Known-good TWRP for walleye got the same words from fastboot boot (Android SE), and one XDA report says it appeared randomly and went away on restart. Our slot flags (a unbootable, current b) were left by the first try; whether they feed the refusal is not known.
5. "Booting OKAY" then silence (a) means the bootloader sent its OK and a later step failed or the kernel died before any sign of life; it is a different outcome from Load Error, and a is the only image that got it. The os word turning OKAY into Load Error says the refusal is sensitive to the header word - the likeliest reason is the bootloader comparing the os_version/patch level with the active slot's recorded one (not read anywhere; unknown).

Ranked causes (each has a try that tells it apart): (H1) overlay merge fails against a mainline base, so a stub dtbo or a dtb that survives the stock overlay is needed - only fixable by a write (dtbo_b stub) or by finding that slot b's dtbo is not the cause; (H2) dtb ids: msm-id only, no board-id/pmic-id; free to test on the host; (H3) state: slot flags or random Load Error; test with a control image; (H4) header word: only os word 0 passes, so keep 0.
Control first: a stock-format image known to boot on walleye (LineageOS or TWRP recovery for walleye, public) through the same fastboot boot path. If the control also gets Load Error, the cause is the phone's state and no image change helps; if it boots, the cause is in our image and the variants below tell which part. The control is a try, not a write.
Not read yet and worth reading without writing: walleye's stock boot.img header and dtb ids from a public LineageOS wahoo build (host only), slot b's dtbo overlay ids (pstore/Android adb read - keeper only).

brief: Load Error is not the slot flags (control refused on a too); the one accepted try came with healthy Android on a, so the next test restores that state, then cold restart, host checks, UART
found:
What is: the control (LineageOS 22.2 20261113 boot.img, stock header, AVB footer, own dtb) is refused with "Failed to load/authenticate boot image: Load Error" on slot b and, per walleye-control-on-slot-a-try, on slot a too; so are our b-f. Seen to be accepted: our boot-b on the very first try (slot a active, phone entered fastboot from healthy Android): the phone left USB, Android came up on b, a flagged unbootable; and boot-a, "Booting OKAY" with nothing starting, on slot b. The same image was refused later. So the refusal is not the image's format and, after the slot-a try, not the active slot or the unbootable flag alone. The same string and A/B flip are reported for walleye since 2017 (XDA PSA); on other Qualcomm ABL phones it comes "randomly" and goes with a restart, another port or cable, set_active or a stock reflash.

Ranked causes now (each by what it predicts):
1. State left by the first tries that set_active does not undo. The one accepted try came from a phone booted into Android on a, with a successful=yes (Android marks it when boot completes). Now a is successful=no, retry 1, and b's flag was reset by our set-active (b successful no). Predicts: after Android boots on a to completion (marks it successful) and the phone is put into the bootloader from that Android, the control is accepted again. Cheapest and reversible; it is the exact first state. Not tested.
2. A bootloader that has stayed up since a failed boot (the 'restart cures it' reports). Predicts: a cold power-off and start into the bootloader, then the same try, is accepted. Not tested; also covered by 1, which reboots the phone.
3. dtbo (or vbmeta) of the active slot. The bootloader picks overlays from dtbo by id and rev and refuses if none fits (AOSP DTO; the taimen bootloader wants id 2704, kcxt). Slot b's is an older Lineage build's and a's is current, yet both refuse, so a mismatch with the new dtb is unlikely; a cause only if 1 and 2 fail. A write; stays named, with no way back for the stock dtbo (fastboot cannot read it back).
4. Host: old fastboot, USB port, cable. The transfer succeeds and the refusal comes back at "booting", so least likely; recorded with each try (fastboot --version).
5. AVB and lock state: the phone reports unlocked yes, where verification errors are warnings; not measured.

Not known yet: the bootloader's own reason. Google's ABL is not public (the CAF Qualcomm ABL only shows the shape) and fastboot has no read-only oem command that prints it. The way to see it is the serial log over the Pixel 2's Android Debug Cable (Nura wiki), which needs the author's hardware.

Vector chosen: restore the first state, since it is the only state in which an image was accepted: set-active a, boot Android on a normally to completion (a's own Android, nothing written), adb reboot bootloader, the control once; then, if still refused, cold power-off start and host checks; then UART; a write last.

brief: Best-known bootstrap: feedback channel first, vendor kernel as known-good, then mainline by fastboot boot; lk2nd is not for MSM8998/ABL; walleye skipped the vendor-kernel step
found:
THE METHOD, in order (pmOS Porting/Mainlining guides, Qualcomm mainline porting, Halium early-init, MSM8998 pages): 1 unlock, keep the stock boot.img and a way back to Android; read offsets/ids from it. 2 Get a feedback channel BEFORE mainline: UART first, then simple-framebuffer, ramoops last (pmOS order); for a no-display phone the USB gadget shell is the channel. 3 Vendor kernel first as a known-good: Halium/UBports/Droidian boot the vendor kernel with their own initramfs (telnet 192.168.2.15, break= levels) - it proves image format, offsets, cmdline, gadget, and shows ids, rails, reserved memory. pmOS recommends a downstream port as the base but no MSM8998 sibling did it; they went straight to mainline. 4 Board dts from msm8998-mtp: fix model/compatible/board-id, delete CoreSight nodes, match regulators, clk_ignore_unused (still the normal first flag, Dybcio 2025). 5 Image.gz + dtb appended, mkbootimg base 0 page 4096, initramfs with debug-shell and USB gadget; fastboot boot (OnePlus 5, Mi 6, Pixel 3 XL with a stub dtbo; OnePlus 5T OxygenOS 9 cannot fastboot boot - flash instead). 6 First shell over USB peripheral (QMP + QUSB2 PHY, dr_mode peripheral); Pixel 2 XL reached exactly this, black screen. 7 Then UFS (not on Sony), display, touch, radios; upstream with b4.
LK2ND: not a route. Its device list stops at msm8996, msm8998 is '?' in targets.md, no Pixel, and it is an LK fork loaded by LK-based aboot; Pixel 2 runs a Qualcomm ABL/UEFI-derived bootloader. Pixel 3/sdm845 recipe is plain fastboot boot plus a stub dtbo, not lk2nd. U-Boot as second stage under ABL exists for sdm845 (FOSDEM 2024), not known for msm8998. Whether an LK image could run under ABL is not known yet.
WALLEYE LANE vs THE METHOD: done - stock ids and header read from the public LineageOS image, boot images a-f (17 checks), gadget initramfs proven in QEMU, minimal dts, control test, and the finding that Load Error follows the slot's successful flag (control accepted only from the first state). Gaps: (a) step 3 never done - no image has run a kernel on this phone, so cmdline, ids, rails, ramoops address, and the gadget on real hardware are unseen; (b) step 2 - no feedback channel chosen: UART needs a cable and an oem decision, ramoops address unverified, simplefb unlikely (command-mode DSC panel); (c) the order: the lane went to its own mainline image before any known-good boot. The control (LineageOS boot.img, vendor 4.4 kernel) is accepted from the first state but then left USB with no sign for 6+ min, so even a stock image gives no feedback on this phone yet.
NOT KNOWN YET: whether the vendor kernel in the control reaches a configfs gadget (LineageOS kernels normally do for adb); whether fastboot oem uart enable persists; walleye's dtbo overlay id; first-shell method on taimen (flash vs fastboot boot); sm8150 practice and the FOSDEM 2024 slides were not read. pmOS wiki now at wiki.nura.eco behind a bot wall; read as raw wikitext.

brief: Our dtb has no __symbols__; the dtbo overlay (idx 3) needs 137 labels, so it cannot merge: fdtoverlay fails on ours, passes on stock. Fits s3 'Booting OKAY' then fastboot.
found:
What is: androidboot.dtbo_idx=3 (set by the bootloader) = dtbo.img entry 3 (id 0x1bc rev 3), 147 fragments, label-targeted, __fixups__ naming 137 labels of the base dtb (cci, tlmm, soc, mdss_mdp, pm8998_gpios...). No msm-id/board-id in the overlays; the entry is picked by id/rev, then merged into the dtb of the boot image.
Measured on the host (material: dtbo-measurements.md): fdtoverlay merges entry 3 into the stock dtb (986 symbols, all 137 present) and FAILS on ours: no /__symbols__ node. AOSP's libufdt, the reference for Android's overlay merge, treats that as an error (aosp-libufdt-overlay). brief: FunctionFS cannot carry CDC functional descriptors, but cdc_acm binds one class-2 interface with 3 endpoints: the helper declares that, writes ep0 before the UDC bind, bridges to a pty shell
found:
What is: the running kernel is the stock 4.4.302 with our ramdisk (research walleye-vendor-kernel-facts-s1-panic): USB_CONFIGFS and F_FS =y, ACM/SERIAL/ECM/RNDIS not set, no devtmpfs, UDC a800000.dwc3. Android itself uses ffs.adb in configfs group g1 on this phone (src-wahoo-init-hardware-usb-rc), so F_FS is exercised by the stock stack.

Finding 1 (the trap): f_fs's descriptor parser (v4.4.302 and v7.3 alike) rejects any descriptor type outside interface, endpoint, HID, OTG, interface-association and SS-companion; CS_INTERFACE (0x24, the CDC header/call-management/ACM/union descriptors) falls to default -> -EINVAL. The queued idea of declaring the full CDC functional descriptors would make the write to ep0 fail.

Finding 2 (the way): cdc_acm's probe, with no union descriptor and a class 2 / subclass 2 / protocol 1 interface with exactly three endpoints, assumes a single combined interface and picks interrupt-in, bulk-in, bulk-out with usb_find_common_endpoints. So ONE interface (class 0x02, sub 0x02, proto 0x01) with interrupt-in (10 bytes, interval 9), bulk-out and bulk-in (512 HS/SS, 64 FS) plus SS companion descriptors is enough; the host gives /dev/ttyACM0. Line coding / control-line-state are best-effort for the host.

Design: (1) init: mount configfs; gadget with ids and strings as n2; functions/ffs.acm, configs/c.1 symlink; mkdir /dev/ffs; mount -t functionfs acm /dev/ffs (no devtmpfs: nodes by cpio; ep0 appears in the ffs mount, ep1..3 after the descriptors are written; /dev/ptmx a cpio node, mount devpts). (2) helper (C, static aarch64, clang, GPL base ffs-test.c, libc only): open /dev/ffs/ep0; write the V2 descriptors blob (flags FS|HS|SS), then the strings blob (lang 0x0409); only then write the UDC name (before that the configfs bind returns -ENODEV: f_fs desc_ready). (3) ep0 loop: on ENABLE open ep1..ep3 (names follow descriptor order) and fork a pty shell (posix_openpt, /bin/sh as session leader); on DISABLE/UNBIND close and kill; answer class SETUP events (SET_LINE_CODING 0x20, GET_LINE_CODING 0x21, SET_CONTROL_LINE_STATE 0x22) with a zero-length ack or canned 115200 8N1 so cdc_acm sees no stall; any other setup gets a stall. (4) bridge: poll pty master and ep2 (bulk-out) -> ep3 (bulk-in); ep1 opened and idle. A bulk-in write blocks until the host reads, so use a thread or timeout so a missing host never hangs the shell; log to /dev/kmsg only on state changes. (5) the mass-storage log window stays the second channel.

Failure modes and how each looks: UDC write ENODEV (descriptors not written first, or parse -EINVAL: helper reports errno on /dev/kmsg and the mass-storage window); enumerates but no ttyACM (host cdc_acm rejected: host dmesg); enumerates then drops (ep0 events unanswered: host reset); panic (as 5b, an unwritten function attribute: this design writes no function attribute, only ep0 data) - the bootloader falls back to slot a as before.

brief: Why a failed fastboot boot flipped the Pixel 2's slots, how to restore, how to keep tries from flipping them
found:
Probable, not proven: the Pixel 2's bootloader is Qualcomm-derived ABL (Google's build is not public). In Qualcomm's ABL source (CAF pie mirror, QcomModulePkg FastbootCmds.c, PartitionTableUpdate.c, avb/VerifiedBoot.c), `fastboot boot` runs LoadImageAndAuth on the active slot; when that fails, HandleActiveSlotUnbootable sets slot a's unbootable flag (leaving successful set - the odd pair we saw), makes b active because b is successful, and cold-resets before the reply (our "Status read failed"). So our kernel probably never ran, and panic=10 is not the cause. `fastboot boot` does not decrement retry-count; a kernel crash falls back to a normal boot of the stock boot partition; a slot that is successful=yes is never counted down.
set_active X (ABL source): makes the slot active at priority 3, retry 7, clears unbootable and successful; swaps the a/b partition-type GUIDs and switches the UFS boot LUN: metadata only, undone by set_active back. a stays successful=no until Android on a marks itself good. `--slot` is ignored by `boot`.
Pixel 2 reports: loops end in "Slot Unbootable: Load Error", fixed by set_active (UBports forum 5639); after 7 unsuccessful boots the bootloader switches slot (pmaports MR 3190); the Pixel 2 XL bootloader refuses a kernel unless dtbo holds overlay id 2704 (kcxt dtbo README) - the likely real cause of the failed authentication, unconfirmed for walleye.
Not known yet: the real failure point; why try a stayed in fastboot and whether it changed flags; why b shows retry 0 after the switch; whether Google's ABL matches Qualcomm's.
Ways: leave flags and try on b (no write; if b is flagged too, set_active is the way out); set_active a now (a stays successful=no, the next failed try flips again); set_active before each try (a write per try); flash a stub dtbo to the active slot (a write, no known way back: the stock dtbo cannot be read back by fastboot); image changes (os_version 0 in our header untested).

brief: A tool is followed by a pin, not files: device parts live beside it as data, hooks or a rust-script on the pinned library; rhizoid carries the cutting and slice cases and lacks three things.
found:
The question: a home for bring-up tools must also let device repositories use them, extend them with device-specific parts, send useful changes back and pull updates in, their own changes side by side with no rebase each time (the author's words, relayed by the coordinator; the problem git-rhizoid was started for). Extends research bringup-tools-landscape.
What is: the chain already decided (idealkb decision 2026-11-17-chain-follow-by-slice, research chain-follow-world): one pin-and-follow mechanism for data and briefs - a source names its generic files, a follower pins a release and keeps its own files, a changed generic file ends follow.sh with exit 3 and goes back as an upstream item (ikb upstream-item, form patch), weekly update-pins and a release gate; device bases follow idealkb and device-template that way. It lays a slice of files. Rhizoid (git-rhizoid.github.io, rhizoid repo) is for whole forks: a cutting is a fork owned and pinned, tracking branch pristine, patch branch merged from it, rhizoid's own metadata additive-only, so a diff of patch against tracking is a clean patch back; its CLI is typed but add/update/status are stubbed, its consumption side is open (design-consumption-side) and slice-consumption was added 2026-11-17 by the idealkb chain. devlab and lpoco-health already reach consumers as released packages (release-plz tags, the packaging conveyor), not as copied files.
Finding: a tool is not a slice. Compiled logic is followed by a version pin, not by files laid into the follower, so the rebase trouble does not arise for the tool at all as long as a device never edits the tool's tree: its own parts live in its own repository, beside the tool, in three levels. (1) Data: device.toml [boot] and the files it names (initramfs skeleton, dtb variants). (2) Hooks: executables the manifest names for a step (shell where stupid simple), called with the paths in arguments, a nonzero exit stops the job. (3) Logic: a rust-script file (or a small crate) in the device repository whose header depends on bringup's library at the pinned tag (rust-script and cargo take a git tag as a dependency). Only two things then need the follow machinery: the pin (a version line the follower owns) and the slice of files that go with the tool in device-template (the [boot] skeleton, hook examples). Sending back: a generic improvement is a pull request to lab-tools from the device's branch, recorded in the device base as an upstream item (form patch) against a lab-tools upstream row seeded beside idealkb and device-template; an update comes by a pin bump (the weekly job, a pull request per source). Side by side: the device's changes are files of its own, so a pin bump touches none of them; when a device must patch the tool itself before upstream takes it, that is a cutting of lab-tools consumed as a git dependency (Cargo [patch]) - rhizoid's exact case, rare because the three levels cover most.
Where rhizoid carries it, and what it lacks (recorded on its own backlog, git-rhizoid.github.io PR 28, not worked around): a cutting consumed by a language manager - writing and bumping the pin where cargo or rust-script reads it (cutting-as-cargo-dependency); one pin file, one bump, one verdict for slices, cuttings and tool versions together (followers-one-pin-bump); sending a patch back as a pull request on the person's word with the follower's own record of it (send-back-writes-the-upstream-item); and slice-consumption (already open) for the template files. Until rhizoid has them: idealkb's follow.sh and update-pins for the slices, a plain fork with a [patch] line for the rare cutting, recorded as a problem.
Not known yet: whether bringup's library API can stay stable enough for the third level while it is 0.x (the first builder's test of pin refusal tells); whether a host binary release (asset) or cargo install --git is the simpler install for a device lab (bringup-release settles it).
question: How do device repositories use, extend, send back to and update from a tools home, side by side with no rebase, and where does rhizoid fit?

brief: abootimg-oxide 0.5.2 writes the v0 header byte for byte as mkbootimg; the id (SHA-1 of three parts) and trailing padding are the caller's
found: Measured 2026-11-17 with a scratch program against mkbootimg (android-tools, header v0, base 0, kernel 0x8000, ramdisk 0x1000000, tags 0x100, page 4096): the crate's header write gave bytes identical to mkbootimg for the whole length it wrote. Two gaps, both ours to fill: (1) full_write only seeks to boot_image_size, so the image ends before the last page's padding (15288 of 16384 bytes) - pack pads itself; (2) the header id: mkbootimg's v0 id is SHA-1 over kernel, ramdisk and second, each followed by its u32 size (three parts), while the crate's compute_hash_digest hashes five (adds recovery dtbo and dtb) - so for v0 the id is computed in our code. With both, pack equals mkbootimg for the plain header and with os_version/os_patch_level words (tests/pack_v0.rs, two cases). mkbootimg writes second address 0 when there is no second image, whatever second_offset says. Header::parse reads v0..v2 and v3/v4; this tool reads v0 only for now. Cost: binrw and thiserror come with the crate. Not known yet: v1/v2 write parity, vendor_boot.
question: Does abootimg-oxide write header v0 byte-exact, or must pack wrap mkbootimg?

brief: No tool does build, swap and check of a boot image in Rust; the parts exist (header, cpio, dtb, compression) and the oracles are mkbootimg and avbtool, so we wrap.
found:
What is: walleye's bring-up is 8 POSIX shell scripts (~520 lines) in google-walleye-lab/build plus tests/host/gadget-up.sh; they call mkbootimg, unpack_bootimg and avbtool (Python from android-tools), the kernel's gen_init_cpio, lz4, fdtget/fdtdump, with their own checks (check-bootimg, check-bisect count fields and fail). Their knowledge is worth keeping: header v0 offsets by variant, the appended dtb, the lz4 frame shape of the stock kernel, the AVB hash footer (algorithm NONE, padded to the control's size), the NET=43 address rewrite, xz because the 4.4 kernel has no gzip. surya's bring-up had no scripts (by hand). Earlier records already decided the family: backlog rust-toolset (one Rust toolset in lab-tools, rust-script for small scripts, pmbootstrap read as reference) and decision 2026-11-17-health-checks-shell-and-rust (shell for plain readings, Rust for logic, rust-script for prototypes and one-offs).
Others: nothing covers the whole job. Android's mkbootimg/unpack_bootimg/repack_bootimg and avbtool (Python) are the authoritative oracles; magiskboot (Rust+C++, GPL) has the model of swapping one part (unpack to a directory, change, repack with the original as template) but is aimed at rooting; abootimg-oxide 0.5.2 (Rust, MIT/Apache, 2026-06) reads and writes header v0-v4 and vendor_boot; abootcrafter has an update flow, no AVB; abl-exorcist (Rust, GPL) shells out to mkbootimg; no AVB crate exists on crates.io (avbroot, GPL, does vbmeta, is no library). Rust crates for the rest: cpio 0.4.2 (newc writer), flate2, lz4_flex (maintained), dtoolkit 0.5.0 (Google, dtb read/edit, young), fdt (read). pmbootstrap is Python, ~24k lines in 129 files; its deviceinfo names (header_version, base, kernel_offset, ramdisk_offset, tags_offset, pagesize, cmdline) are the vocabulary to reuse; the boot image is not built there. Mobian, Droidian (initramfs-tools-halium: shell hooks for an initramfs only), lk2nd (a bootloader, no host tooling): nothing to take. No tool checks an image against expected header fields; unpack_bootimg plus a comparison is all there is, which is what our check scripts do.
Not known yet: whether abootimg-oxide writes byte-identical v0 images; dtoolkit's maturity; whether cpio 0.4.2 reads; whether boot-deploy, Mobian and Halium scripts add anything (not read; the outside look was done by a read-only researcher from page summaries, so counts are weaker than a source read).
Where tools live today: lab-tools (its README: tools for bringing up and testing Linux phones, not tied to one device) is the one place already: devlab (the phone: fastboot, flash, kernel try, provision, keeper, health, MCP; 5.4k lines with rmcp and tokio), health (runs on the phone) and tone. Device repos hold data and thin scripts.

brief: The AOP's view is not readable from Linux; the flush is sound; peers on near-mainline never read the counters as good either, so standby current, not aosd, is the arbiter
found:
(1) Does the AOP get the flush. The entry trace already shows the Apps RSC writes wake and sleep sets in one instant on the last CPU and then requests the deepest cluster state (0x4100b244), so Linux's half is done in order. The AOP's half is not observable from Linux: the only outputs are the counters it fills (aosd, cxsd, ddr in the message RAM) and the rails. Nothing in mainline reads an AOP log. What the AOP needs for cxsd is every master's sleep vote on CX gone (Apps, modem, adsp, cdsp, display, WLAN BB), not only Apps'. A peer found exactly that kind of cause: on SM7325 a WLAN BB vote prevented CX power collapse (CXPC) and, once removed, "HLOS and DDR votes remain" (pmaports#4846, 2026-11-16); on SM8550 an SD-controller IRQ storm and a USB PHY vote did (armada#274). So the entry is not the open question any more; the other masters' votes and the wakeups are.

(2) Why the cluster genpd S2idle column stays 0. From core.c: usage_s2idle is incremented only in genpd_sync_power_off, after the domain's governor (pm_domain_cpu_gov, set by cpuidle-psci-domain only when the domain has idle states) approved the power-down, and that function returns early unless every device attached to the cluster domain has been suspended (suspended_count == device_count) and every child CPU domain is off. s2idle reaches it through dev_pm_genpd_suspend, not runtime PM. The trace shows the cluster bits in the PSCI state (0x4100b244), so the cluster power-off callback did run; then either the counter is read from the wrong row/domain, or the state composed is from a path that did not count. Both are cheap to tell apart and are not known yet: read idle_states of every power-domain-* after one cycle (all rows, all columns) and the psci_domain_idle_enter trace's s2idle flag.

(3) Is the SoC asleep already, and the arbiter. The peer record says the counters are not the whole picture: motorola-dubai (SM7325) reads S2 for ~1 ms, and the author of the qclaptops tree removed WLAN BB, touch, audio and regulator holders with "idle drain lowered by 0.00000 W". The same report measures current_now: near-mainline 152 mA (later 60 mA, 0.2-0.3 W), the same-era Droidian downstream kernel on xiaomi-miatoll (SM6250) 9 mA. So a number exists to match: about 9 mA average with screen off on a Snapdragon 6/7-series phone running the vendor kernel. Android's own number on surya is not known yet: nobody has measured it, and the public sources give no standby current (android-reference).

(4) Cheaper tools than the AOP: regulator_summary (what rails stay on, with users), pm_genpd_summary, qcom_stats, and current_now / charge_counter. Android's value is the end, regulators the where.

brief: Counters look valid; SH0 is not shown to block (awake icc read is not the flush moment); the unread facts are the RSC flush, last-CPU idle state and IRQ rate at entry
found:
Question 1, counter validity: the counters are very probably valid. qcom_stats creates its files by reading each record's name word out of the message RAM (qcom_stats.c), and surya has aosd, cxsd and ddr: three names read, not assumed. ddr_stats also passed its magic key, and its frequency rows move while the LPM rows stay 0 (research floor-holders), so the block is live and the layout is the one sc7180 uses, where the Acer Aspire 1 counts. adsp 0 and empty apss/display/gpu are SMEM entries this firmware does not fill; they are not the SoC counters. Not found anywhere: an Android reading of these counters on SM7150 (no source, none observed). Only an independent measure can make the last doubt certain: standby current (sleep-standby-current).

Question 2, is SH0 x=1,y=3 the blocker: not shown, and the reading rests on a mix-up that is worth fixing. bcm-voter.c forces keepalive BCMs only in the AMC and WAKE buckets, so a SLEEP-bucket x=1,y=3 means some request with a SLEEP-bearing tag (ALWAYS = 7) had non-zero bandwidth at the flush. The awake icc summary is not that moment: the only large vote there is USB (240000 = USB_MEMORY_AVG_HS_BW in dwc3-qcom.c, tag 7) and dwc3_qcom_suspend sets it to 0 before the last CPU flushes; the peak is cpu0/cpu6 at tag 3 (AMC|WAKE, not SLEEP). So the vote that makes x=1,y=3 is one nobody has seen being made: not USB as a floor holder (UDC unbound: counters 0 -> 0; whether SH0 changed was not read), not uart8, not the cpufreq votes by tag. Two readings remain and they cannot be told apart by subtracting: (a) the flush the log shows is stale or not the last one, i.e. the sleep set is not what the AOP sees at entry; (b) SH0 is harmless and something else blocks. So SH0 is demoted from "the blocker" to "one unexplained entry"; no more owner-hunting by tag until the entry is read.

What is the blocker then: the three observations nobody has taken at the entry itself. (1) Is the RSC flush invoked on the last CPU and what does it write (tracepoints rpmh_send_msg state=sleep; rpmh_rsc_cpu_pm_callback flushes at CPU_PM_ENTER of the last online CPU). (2) What the last CPU's idle state is (power:cpu_idle with the PSCI state, per-CPU cpuidle usage/time deltas): a cycle can "take" the cluster state once and still wake every few ms. (3) Whether anything wakes the CPUs during the 15 s: /proc/interrupts delta. This last one is what the nearest measured sibling found: on the Odin 2 (SM8550) suspend succeeded, counters read 0, and the cause was an SD controller firing ~30 irq/s through the whole suspend plus a USB PHY vote and CPU0 idle disabled (armada#274). The Qualcomm guide's own order for "aosd count zero" is also: display off, USB disconnected, suspend success count, then wake locks. Surya has never had its interrupt rate read across a cycle; devlab-usb is also a wakeup source active the whole time (research floor-holders).

Question 3, what a late-suspend dump should read: per-CPU cpuidle state usage/time before and after; the cluster genpd idle_states usage (taken, rejected) and the time spent; the sleep-set commands written (trace rpmh); /proc/interrupts delta; wakeup_sources; suspend_stats; qcom_stats of all nodes before and after (including each subsystem's last-entered time). All of it is tracefs/procfs/debugfs: no kernel build is needed, so floor-suspend-late-dump (a debug kernel) is not first.
Also AOP QMP: the AOP does process RSC commands (regulators, rpmhpd and icc work), so it is alive; QMP is a separate channel and, as found, off the path.
Sources read, not run on the phone; nothing on the phone was touched.

SH0 is not a holder someone took; it is a keepalive BCM. In mainline sm7150.c, bcm_sh0 is "SH0", keepalive, node qns_llcc, identical to sdm845, sm8150 and sc7180 (the sc7180 Acer Aspire 1 reaches cxsd/aosd/ddr counts with the same definition). bcm-voter.c forces keepalive BCMs to x=y=1 (or enable_mask) only in the AMC and WAKE buckets. The SLEEP bucket is aggregated from consumers' tags only, so a sleep-set SH0 x=1,y=3 means a consumer whose tag includes SLEEP (QCOM_ICC_TAG_ALWAYS = AMC|WAKE|SLEEP) has a path through qns_llcc with a tiny bandwidth. In sm7150.dtsi the candidates are the QUP nodes, which use TAG_ALWAYS interconnects (one serial toward gem_noc SLAVE_LLCC, near line 1259), the crypto engine (ALWAYS to EBI, line 460), and uart8 serial@a88000 (the debug UART), which the recorded cycles show at avg 1 peak 1 across suspend. The owner is a DT tag on a consumer, not a firmware latch.
Whether the SH0 sleep vote blocks aosd is NOT known yet: no source shows the sleep-set contents of the Aspire 1 or any SM7150-class phone; SH0 is only the sole non-zero sleep entry on surya, which makes it the cheapest subtraction.
QMP: the aoss_qmp node (c300000, spi 389, mboxes apss_shared 0, apss_shared at 17c00000) is identical to sm8150 and sc7180, so the wiring in the tree is not the difference. Open succeeds, every send times out: the AOP does not clear the length word after the kick; qmp_send gives no other signal. Downstream wiring (irq-reg-base 17c0000c, mask 1) could not be confirmed from a source this session - not known yet. QMP matters only for the aoss prevent knobs (cx_mol, ddr_mol; hypothesis 5, unlikely) and is not on the path to the SH0 owner.
Read from the tree at kernel-rc3; nothing on the phone was touched.
question: What is SH0 x=1,y=3, who votes it, what do SDM845/SM8150/SC7180 do, and why does the AOP not ack QMP?

brief: surya has the qcom_wdt watchdog, 4 MiB ramoops and a PMIC RTC (1970); the stock watchdog is stopped in late suspend, so no way back covers a hang inside s2idle
found: On the phone: qcom_wdt (17c10000.watchdog) with /dev/watchdog0, ramoops 4 MiB reserved at 0x9d800000 with pstore (console 1 MiB), the PMIC RTC reading 1970 and settable with hwclock -w -u; the kernel has no suspend timeout of its own (no PM_DEBUG, hung-task, DPM watchdog). Mainline qcom-wdt.c registers late system sleep ops that STOP an active watchdog in suspend and start it on resume: so a hang before the late phase is covered by a watchdog, one inside s2idle is not. A module with that stop made optional (one parameter, no other change) builds for the running kernel (no MODVERSIONS; vermagic equals uname -r) and loads without a kernel rebuild or reboot-to-test; a reboot undoes it. The RTC alarm cannot be the way back: if the RTC wake does not reach the GIC out of s2idle the phone sleeps for good, which looks the same as a hang. A bite resets the SoC; whether it reaches a normal boot and whether ramoops survives it is what the dry run measures.

brief: What made the TX decimator to codec DMA path deliver zeros, and what does a capture of zeros tell?
found: The decimator-to-DSP leg worked all along: each silent recording began with ~0.5 s of ringing (-1774 settling to exact 0), the high-pass filter draining a constant input - the decimator ran and its output reached TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3, but no samples entered it. The cause was upstream of the decimator: the capture link named the TX SoundWire controller's DAI 0, its playback DAI (qcom_swrm_register_dais makes the first num_dout_ports DAIs playback, and this controller has one dout port), so sdw_stream_add_master was never called and the codec's ports never programmed. The same one-dout-port shift moves master port numbers by one (ports start at 2; swr2's qcom,ports-* arrays begin with 0xff). For DMICs the same reading held: with no clock on the pin the data line is static and the filter removes it. So: start-up ringing then exact zeros means no input reaches the decimator - look at the source (SoundWire stream, DMIC clock), not the DMA or the AFE port. The AFE port is the vendor's too: TX AIF1 on TX_CDC_DMA_TX_3 (45111 = 0xB037), accepted by this ADSP.
question: What made the TX decimator to codec DMA path deliver zeros, and what does a capture of zeros tell?

brief: Why does nothing come back from surya's main microphone, now that the WCD9375 enumerates and the sound card is made?
found: The codec dropped off both SoundWire buses because ASoC puts every idle component into its sleep pin state, and the codec's sleep state drove its active-low reset low (traced: snd_soc_bind_card committed it 0.24 ms before both interfaces went UNATTACHED). Without a sleep state the codec stays attached and capture prepares (linux-phone-oco/linux PR #4); the SoundWire pin-mux fix is PR #3. Capture still yields exact zeros: the built-in microphones are digital mics (vendor: TX DMIC1-3 on LPI gpio26-29, function 1, mic bias 1 and 3); this ADSP rejects the VA capture port, so they go through the TX macro to TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3; with the VA DMIC clocks forced on the TX path still reads zeros, as it does from ADC1 - the next fault sits in the TX decimator to DSP leg. Details: research/microphone.md.

brief: Why does the ADSP sensors service crash-loop the audio DSP on surya, and what would stop it without changing the firmware?
found: Measured on the phone (read only, kept kernel 7.1.0-sm7150-calls+, 2026-11-17) and read in hexagonrpcd's source. At start the DSP's registry sensor compares each config it knows (the registry's sns_reg_config: 47 configs, every one recorded with data 1230768000 - 2009-01-01, Android's fixed vendor mtime) with the config files hexagonrpcd serves, and hexagonrpcd passes their real mtime: all 46 on the phone carry 1779945838 (the package's build time), and sns_pickup.json is listed but absent. Every config therefore looks changed, the DSP re-parses and writes (temp.json), hexagonrpcd refuses every write by design, and the DSP asserts (SNS_REG_INIT, sns_registry_sensor.c) and restarts with audio. The version marker sns_reg_version, whose absence also forces a rebuild elsewhere (hexagonrpc #19), cannot be served at all: the virtual persist/sensors/registry holds only its registry subdirectory. So no trial of 2026-11-09 had both conditions of an untouched registry - the marker reached and the configs unchanged; they disproved only a registry swap. Hypothesis to settle first: configs touched to 1230768000 (and no listed config missing) make the pre-parsed registry current, so nothing is written and the ADSP stays up. Independent of it: the same assert is open upstream on X1P42100 (#29, 2026-11-14) and was stopped by writes elsewhere (#19, #27).

brief: Does sm7150's device tree ask the firmware for the cluster states surya's firmware knows?
found: Apparently not, for the two deepest. sm7150.dtsi (sm7150-mainline, the same in our tree) carries three cluster states whose latencies are surya's own but whose PSCI parameters are SC7180's: 0x41000044 (cluster power collapse), 0x41001244 and 0x4100b244. surya's own Android device tree (lpm-levels, cluster mode shifted by 4) has l3-pc 0x4, cx-off 0x224 and llcc-off 0xc24 - that is 0x41000044, 0x41002244 and 0x4100c244; 0x4100c244 is also what SM8150, the closest sibling, uses for its one cluster sleep. On the phone the deepest state (0x4100b244) was never entered once at runtime. Whether the firmware rejects, demotes or honours SC7180's values is not known: it is the first thing a measured suspend settles. SM7150 is not yet in mainline: the 2025 upstreaming series is to be resent, so a correction can go into it.

brief: Standby drain is made a repeatable test, scored as average current from the charge counter delta; no standard 'suitcase test' exists
found: Yes, repeatable - but scored as mean current, not battery percent. Observed (Android power-component guide, source.android.com/docs/core/power/component): measure suspend with no wakelocks, confirm the device really suspends, wait for the reading to settle, average radio current over time, unplug USB first (a host can feed current). GameBench: hourly drain = capacity / average current. No standard 'suitcase test' or 'overnight drain test' found; the name is ours. pmaports#4846 (motorola-dubai 17x Droidian; method unread). Droidian miatoll 9 mA: its method not found; PinePhone anecdotes are single reports. Inference: charge_counter delta over the whole window is the primary number, current_now only a cross-check (wake samples inflate it), the gauge percentage least trustworthy. brief: Why does the modem not go online once a SIM card is in?
found: With the SIM in (operator 1&1, card present and ready) the modem refuses every request to go online: its own operating mode reads shutting-down from the start of boot, and ModemManager gets DeviceNotReady. The identity does not: a table is kept as another kind of thing than a lens, though it is the passthrough of what a place keeps. A lens's two faces, glimpse and focus, are put and get, but their law is nowhere said - one sign of it shows by accident: a table nothing brings into focus.
